{{about|representing a non-negative polynomial as sum of squares of polynomials|representing a polynomial as a sum of squares of rational functions|Hilbert's seventeenth problem|the sum of squares of consecutive integers|square pyramidal number|representing an integer as a sum of squares of integers|Lagrange's four-square theorem}}

In [[mathematics]], a [[homogeneous polynomial|form]] (i.e. a homogeneous polynomial) ''h''(''x'') of [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] 2''m'' in the [[real number|real]] ''n''-dimensional vector ''x'' is sum of squares of forms (SOS) [[if and only if]] there exist forms <math>g_1(x),\ldots,g_k(x)</math> of degree ''m'' such that
<math display="block">h(x) = \sum_{i=1}^k g_i(x)^2 .</math>

Every form that is SOS is also a [[positive polynomial]], although the [[converse (logic)|converse]] is not always true in general. In the special cases of ''n'' = 2 and 2''m'' = 2, or ''n'' = 3 and 2''m'' = 4, [[Hilbert]] proved that a form is SOS if and only if it is positive.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hilbert|first1=David|title=Ueber die Darstellung definiter Formen als Summe von Formenquadraten|journal=Mathematische Annalen|date=September 1888|volume=32|issue=3|pages=342–350|doi=10.1007/bf01443605|s2cid=177804714 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1428214}}</ref> The same is also true for the analogous problem with positive ''symmetric'' forms.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Choi|first1=M. D.|last2=Lam|first2=T. Y.|author2-link=Tsit Yuen Lam|title=An old question of Hilbert|journal=Queen's Papers in Pure and Applied Mathematics|date=1977|volume=46|pages=385–405}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Goel|first1=Charu|last2=Kuhlmann|first2=Salma|last3=Reznick|first3=Bruce|title=On the Choi–Lam analogue of Hilbert's 1888 theorem for symmetric forms|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|date=May 2016|volume=496|pages=114–120|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2016.01.024|arxiv=1505.08145|s2cid=17579200 |author3-link=Bruce Reznick}}</ref>

Although not every form is SOS, there are efficiently testable sufficient conditions for a form to be SOS.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lasserre|first1=Jean B.|title=Sufficient conditions for a real polynomial to be a sum of squares| journal=Archiv der Mathematik|volume=89|issue=5|pages=390–398|doi=10.1007/s00013-007-2251-y|url=http://www.optimization-online.org/DB_HTML/2007/02/1587.html|arxiv=math/0612358|year=2007|s2cid=9319455 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| last1=Powers|first1=Victoria|author1-link=Victoria Powers|last2=Wörmann|first2=Thorsten|title=An algorithm for sums of squares of real polynomials|journal=Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra|date=1998|volume=127|issue=1|pages=99–104| doi=10.1016/S0022-4049(97)83827-3| url=http://www.mathcs.emory.edu/~vicki/pub/sos.pdf|doi-access=free}}</ref> Moreover, every real nonnegative form can be approximated as closely as desired (in the <math>l_1</math>-norm of its coefficient vector) by a sequence of forms <math>\{f_\epsilon\}</math> that are SOS.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lasserre|first1=Jean B.|title=A Sum of Squares Approximation of Nonnegative Polynomials|journal=SIAM Review|date=2007|volume=49|issue=4|pages=651–669|doi=10.1137/070693709|arxiv=math/0412398|bibcode=2007SIAMR..49..651L}}</ref>

== Square matricial representation (SMR) ==
To establish whether a form {{math|''h''(''x'')}} is SOS amounts to solving a [[convex optimization]] problem. Indeed, any {{math|''h''(''x'')}} can be written as
<math display="block">h(x) = (x^{\{m\}})^{T}\left(H+L(\alpha)\right)x^{\{m\}}</math>
where <math>x^{\{m\}}</math> is a vector containing a basis for the space of forms of degree ''m'' in ''x'' (such as all [[monomial]]s of degree ''m''), ''H'' is any [[symmetric matrix]] satisfying <math>h(x) = (x^{\left\{m\right\}})^{T}Hx^{\{m\}}</math>,
and <math>L(\alpha)</math> is a linear parameterization of the [[linear subspace]]
<math display="block">\mathcal{L} = \left\{L=L':~x^{\{m\}'} L x^{\{m\}}=0\right\}.</math>

The dimension of the vector <math>x^{\{m\}}</math> is given by
<math display="block">\sigma(n,m) = \binom{n+m-1}{m},</math>
whereas the dimension of the vector <math>\alpha</math> is given by
<math display="block">\omega(n,2m) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma(n,m)\left(1+\sigma(n,m)\right)-\sigma(n,2m).</math>

The polynomial {{math|''h''(''x'')}} is SOS if and only if there exists a vector <math>\alpha</math> such that
<math>H + L(\alpha)</math> is a [[positive-semidefinite matrix]]. This is a [[linear matrix inequality]] (LMI), and the existence of <math>\alpha</math> is a [[convex optimization|convex feasibility problem]].

The expression <math>h(x)=x^{\{m\}'}\left(H+L(\alpha)\right)x^{\{m\}}</math> was introduced with the name square matricial representation (SMR) in order to establish whether a form is SOS via an LMI.<ref>{{cite conference |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7099515 |title=On convexification of some minimum distance problems |last1=Chesi |first1=G. |last2=Tesi |first2=A. |last3=Vicino |first3=A. |last4=Genesio |first4=R.  |date=1999 |publisher=IEEE |book-title=Proceedings of the 5th European Control Conference |pages=1446–1451 |location=Karlsruhe, Germany}}</ref> The matrix <math>H + L(\alpha)</math> is also known as a [[Gram matrix]].<ref>{{cite conference |title=Sums of squares of real polynomials |last1=Choi |first1=M. |last2=Lam |first2=T. |last3=Reznick |first3=B. |date=1995 |book-title=Proceedings of Symposia in Pure Mathematics |pages=103–125 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/240268385}}</ref>

=== Examples ===

*Consider <math>m = 2</math> and the form <math>h(x)=x_1^4-x_1^2x_2^2+x_2^4</math> of degree 4 in two variables. We have <math display="block">x^{\{m\}} = \begin{pmatrix} x_1^2\\x_1x_2\\x_2^2\end{pmatrix}\!,
~H+L(\alpha) = \begin{pmatrix}
1&0&-\alpha_1\\0&-1+2\alpha_1&0\\-\alpha_1&0&1
\end{pmatrix}\!.</math> Since there exists &alpha; such that <math>H+L(\alpha)\ge 0</math>, namely <math>\alpha=1</math>, it follows that ''h''(''x'') is SOS.
*Consider <math>m = 2</math> and the form <math>h(x)=2x_1^4-5x_1^3x_2/2+x_1^2x_2x_3-2x_1x_3^3+5x_2^4+x_3^4</math> of degree 4 in three variables. We have <math display="block">x^{\{m\}}=\begin{pmatrix}x_1^2\\x_1x_2\\x_1x_3\\x_2^2\\x_2x_3\\x_3^2\end{pmatrix},
~H+L(\alpha) = \begin{pmatrix}
2&-5/4&0&-\alpha_1&-\alpha_2&-\alpha_3\\
-5/4&2\alpha_1&1/2+\alpha_2&0&-\alpha_4&-\alpha_5\\
0&1/2+\alpha_2&2\alpha_3&\alpha_4&\alpha_5&-1\\
-\alpha_1&0&\alpha_4&5&0&-\alpha_6\\
-\alpha_2&-\alpha_4&\alpha_5&0&2\alpha_6&0\\
-\alpha_3&-\alpha_5&-1&-\alpha_6&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.</math> Since <math>H+L(\alpha)\ge 0</math> for <math>\alpha=(1.18,-0.43,0.73,1.13,-0.37,0.57)</math>, it follows that {{math|''h''(''x'')}} is SOS.

== Generalizations and analogs ==

=== Matrix SOS ===
A matrix form ''F''(''x'') (i.e., a matrix whose entries are forms) of dimension ''r'' and degree 2''m'' in the real ''n''-dimensional vector ''x'' is SOS if and only if there exist matrix forms <math>G_1(x),\ldots,G_k(x)</math> of degree ''m'' such that
<math display="block">F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^k G_i(x)^{T}G_i(x) .</math>

==== Matrix SMR ====
To establish whether a matrix form ''F''(''x'') is SOS amounts to solving a convex [[optimization problem]]. Indeed, similarly to the scalar case any ''F''(''x'') can be written according to the SMR as
<math display="block">F(x) = \left(x^{\{m\}}\otimes I_r\right)^{T}\left(H+L(\alpha)\right)\left(x^{\{m\}}\otimes I_r\right)</math>
where <math>\otimes</math> is the [[Kronecker product]] of matrices, ''H'' is any symmetric matrix satisfying
<math display="block">F(x) = \left(x^{\{m\}}\otimes I_r\right)^{T}H\left(x^{\{m\}}\otimes I_r\right)</math>
and <math>L(\alpha)</math> is a linear parameterization of the linear space
<math display="block">\mathcal{L}=\left\{L=L^{T}:~\left(x^{\{m\}}\otimes I_r\right)^{T}L\left(x^{\{m\}}\otimes I_r\right)=0\right\}.</math>

The dimension of the vector <math>\alpha</math> is given by
<math display="block">\omega(n,2m,r)=\frac{1}{2}r\left(\sigma(n,m)\left(r\sigma(n,m)+1\right)-(r+1)\sigma(n,2m)\right).</math>

Then, {{math|''F''(''x'')}} is SOS if and only if there exists a vector <math>\alpha</math> such that the following LMI holds:
<math display="block">H+L(\alpha) \ge 0.</math>

The expression <math>F(x) = \left(x^{\{m\}}\otimes I_r\right)^{T}\left(H+L(\alpha)\right)\left(x^{\{m\}}\otimes I_r\right)</math> was introduced in order to establish whether a matrix form is SOS via an LMI.<ref>{{cite conference |title=Robust stability for polytopic systems via polynomially parameter-dependent Lyapunov functions |last1=Chesi |first1=G. |last2=Garulli |first2=A. |last3=Tesi |first3=A. |last4=Vicino |first4=A. |date=2003 |publisher=IEEE |book-title=Proceedings of the 42nd IEEE Conference on Decision and Control |pages=4670–4675 |location=Maui, Hawaii | doi=10.1109/CDC.2003.1272307 }}</ref>

=== Noncommutative polynomial SOS ===

Consider the [[free algebra]] ''R''⟨''X''⟩ generated by the ''n'' noncommuting letters ''X'' = (''X''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''X''<sub>''n''</sub>) and equipped with the involution {{math|<sup>''T''</sup>}}, such that {{math|<sup>''T''</sup>}} fixes ''R'' and ''X''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''X''<sub>''n''</sub> and reverses words formed by ''X''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''X''<sub>''n''</sub>.
We consider Hermitian noncommutative [[polynomial]]s ''f'', which are the noncommutative polynomials of the form {{math|1=''f'' = ''f''<sup>''T''</sup>}}. When evaluating a Hermitian noncommutative polynomial ''f'' on any ''n''-tuple of real matrices of any size ''r'' × ''r'' produces in a [[positive semi-definite matrix]], ''f'' is said to be matrix-positive.

A noncommutative polynomial is SOS if there exists noncommutative polynomials <math>h_1,\ldots,h_k</math> such that
<math display="block">f(X) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} h_i(X)^T h_i(X).</math>

Surprisingly, in the noncommutative scenario a noncommutative polynomial is SOS if and only if it is matrix-positive.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Helton|first1=J. William|title="Positive" Noncommutative Polynomials Are Sums of Squares|journal=The Annals of Mathematics|date=September 2002|volume=156|issue=2|pages=675–694|doi=10.2307/3597203|jstor=3597203}}</ref> Moreover, there exist algorithms available to decompose matrix-positive polynomials in sum of squares of noncommutative polynomials.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Burgdorf|first1=Sabine|last2=Cafuta|first2=Kristijan|last3=Klep|first3=Igor|last4=Povh|first4=Janez|title=Algorithmic aspects of sums of Hermitian squares of noncommutative polynomials|journal=Computational Optimization and Applications|date=25 October 2012|volume=55|issue=1|pages=137–153|doi=10.1007/s10589-012-9513-8|s2cid=254416733 }}</ref>

=== Polynomial HSOS ===
A complex polynomial <math>p(z_1, \dots, z_n)</math> in variables <math>z_1, \dots, z_n</math> and their conjugates <math>z_1^*, \dots, z_n^*</math> is Hermitian if it takes on only real values, or equivalently if each term has an equal number of conjugated and un-conjugated variables. It is a hermitian sum-of-squares (HSOS) if there are complex polynomials <math>g_1, \dots, g_k</math>, in only the un-conjugated variables <math>z_1, \dots, z_n</math>, such that <math display="block">p(z) = \sum _{i = 1} ^{k} g_i^*(z)g_i(z).</math> A Hermitian square matricial representation of <math>p</math> is a matrix <math>M</math> such that <math>p(z) = (z^{\{m\}})^{*}Mz^{\{m\}}</math>, where <math>(z^{\{m\}})^{*}</math> is the [[Hermitian transpose]] of the vector <math>z^{\{m\}}</math>. As first observed by Putinar, there is a choice of the matrix <math>M</math> having certain symmetry properties, which is in fact unique and can be written explicitly. Thus testing if a Hermitian polynomial is HSOS of degree <math>m</math> can be done by testing if a single, fixed matrix is positive-semidefinite.<ref name="n064">{{cite book | last=Putinar | first=Mihai | title=Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry | chapter=Chapter 9: Sums of Hermitian Squares: Old and New | publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics | publication-place=Philadelphia, PA | date=2012 | isbn=978-1-61197-228-3 | doi=10.1137/1.9781611972290.ch9 | url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611972290.ch9 | page=407–446}}</ref>
